paragraphs.text: Nanophthalmos-4 is an autosomal dominant eye disorder in which both eyes are abnormally small from birth. Affected individuals have short axial lengths and high hyperopia, with no other physical abnormalities. Angle-closure glaucoma may develop later in life, and visual acuity is often reduced (Yu et al., 2009; Awadalla et al., 2014; Khorram et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Yu et al. (2009) described a 5-generation Chinese family with isolated simple microphthalmia. The 9 affected members were aged 6 to 66 years (mean, 42.8 years) and had had bilateral disease since birth. Hyperopia ranged from +4.50 to +11.50 diopters (mean, +8.00), and axial length ranged from 18.22 to 20.26 mm (mean, 19.29 mm). Best corrected visual acuity was less than 0.5 in most eyes. There were no other physical anomalies. Three patients, all older than 50 years, developed angle-closure glaucoma or occludable anterior chamber angles. They were treated by trabeculectomy, but the disease continued to progress, and 2 patients developed atrophia bulbi despite repeated surgeries. One-third of the cases had learning disabilities. The authors noted that thickening of the lens after middle age contributed to refractory glaucoma and that most patients had lost visual acuity by middle age.

paragraphs.text: Yu et al. (2009) also examined sclera from affected family members by histology. The scleral stroma contained diffusely swollen collagen fibers that were twisted or frayed and mixed with normal fibers. In the 2 atrophied globes, collagen fiber alignment was disrupted, with coil-like amorphous material and a sclera 3 times normal thickness. The corneas were also thickened, pigment cells had proliferated, and bone-like tissue had formed.

paragraphs.text: Awadalla et al. (2014) studied a large white family (NNO-SA1), recruited in South Australia, with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. Nanophthalmos was defined as an axial length below 20.0 mm and/or a refractive error above +7.00. Of 35 available family members, 16 (46%) were affected. Affected members had a mean refraction of +11.8 D and a mean axial length of 17.6 mm.

Six of 10 examined members had nanophthalmos, and 3 more were affected according to the family history. Affected individuals had a mean axial eye length of 17.1 +/- 0.31 mm and high hyperopia, with spherical equivalent refractions of about +13 diopters, compared with +0.71 diopters in unaffected relatives.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) performed genomewide SNP linkage analysis in 2 families with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. In pedigree 991-F, a 20.2-Mbp segment of chromosome 17p12-q12 (between rs530664 and rs16523) cosegregated with nanophthalmos. Together these results placed the gene between rs917541 and rs16523, in a region previously linked to autosomal dominant nanophthalmos in a Chinese pedigree.

paragraphs.text: Awadalla et al. (2014) performed whole exome sequencing in the NNO-SA1 family with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. Within the linked region they found a single novel heterozygous missense mutation that segregated with the disease: c.577G-C (ala193-to-pro; A193P), in exon 8 of the TMEM98 gene. The variant was absent from the Exome Variant Server database and from 285 local white controls. RT-PCR showed that TMEM98 was expressed in all ocular tissues tested, including the sclera and the optic nerve head. The authors concluded that TMEM98 was most likely the cause of disease in this family and described it as the first gene identified for autosomal dominant nanophthalmos.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) performed exome sequencing within the chromosome 17 linked region in affected members of a US family with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (pedigree 991-F) and identified a heterozygous his196-to-pro (H196P) missense mutation in the TMEM98 gene, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Of 4 nonsynonymous variants in the linked region, only this one cosegregated with the disease and was absent from healthy relatives. It was predicted to be damaging by SIFT, PolyPhen2, and BLOSUM62, altered a highly conserved histidine, and was absent from the Exome Variant Server and the 1000 Genomes Project.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) also used Sanger sequencing to study a Mariana Islands family with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (pedigree 951-N). In all 11 affected members they identified a heterozygous 34-bp deletion in the TMEM98 gene (c.694_721delAGAATGAAGACTGGATCGAAGATGCCTCgtaagg). The deletion spans the last 28 bp of exon 4 and the first 6 bp of intron 4 and was predicted to eliminate a splice site and cause premature termination. It segregated with the disease, was absent from 4 healthy relatives, and was not found in the Exome Variant Server or the 1000 Genomes Project.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a large white family from South Australia with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (NNO-SA1), Awadalla et al. (2014) used whole exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.577G-C transversion in exon 8 of the TMEM98 gene, resulting in an ala193-to-pro (A193P) substitution. It was the only novel variant in the linked region on chromosome 17p12-q12 that segregated with the disease. The variant was absent from the Exome Variant Server database and from 285 local white controls.
